key: Chaos Theory + Cognitive Load Theory + Neuromodulation

concepts.name: Chaos Theory
concepts.short_description: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions in deterministic systems; strange attractors, Lyapunov exponents.

concepts.name: Cognitive Load Theory
concepts.short_description: Limited working memory constrains learning; intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load; chunking.

concepts.name: Neuromodulation
concepts.short_description: Chemical signals that alter neural circuit dynamics; dopamine, serotonin, gain control, state-dependent processing.

Any perturbation-response (causal intervention) readout recovers a coupling graph whether or not the carrier is chaotic; success would show that intervention beats observation, not that chaos is what measures interactivity. Separately, the global leak may synchronise units so that every readout sees one block.

R strictly not reproduced: grouping 10/10 at ARI 1.0 but correlation control -0.111 (below chance, outside |mean| <= 0.1). ORIG did NOT fire (contracting carrier r=0.2 groups 0/10) -- the author's prediction was wrong. ALT FAILED: non-chaotic levels r=0.65 (Lyapunov -0.92) and r=0.8 group perfectly; the readout tracks carrier amplitude, not chaos.

hypotheses.statement: Capacity-matched chaos: a learner's useful exploration level (largest Lyapunov exponent of its internal dynamics) must be matched to task intrinsic load, and a slow scalar modulator performs the matching. Experiment: vary element interactivity and test whether the optimal modulator setting shifts.

Chunks are attractors carved from a chaotic sea; working-memory capacity is the number of attractors that can coexist before basins crowd, fragment or merge; modulation changes that number. Experiment: count retrievable attractors versus a gain parameter.

Overload is a dynamical phase transition: past a threshold number of held interacting items, the competition among them itself becomes chaotic and items are lost; modulation that weakens interaction shifts the threshold. Experiment: add items one at a time and test whether chaos onset and recall collapse coincide.

Curriculum is a path through a bifurcation diagram: the modulator is the slow bifurcation parameter, and through hysteresis the order in which tasks of different load are met determines the final attractor set. Experiment: same tasks, opposite orders, compare retained structure.

Working-memory span is a predictability horizon: only what can be predicted forward can be held, so span scales with Lyapunov time, and the modulator buys span at the cost of flexibility. Experiment: measure span of a memory held in a chaotic carrier versus lambda_max.

Low-bandwidth control of a high-dimensional chaotic system: a modulator is a scalar broadcast controller, and what it can stabilise is limited by how many past states the controller can hold (its load). Experiment: stabilisable UPO period versus controller memory size.

Learnability of a chaotic source by a capacity-limited chunker peaks at an entropy matched to its chunk budget; the modulator tunes source entropy (or sampling) to that match. Experiment: vary topological entropy and chunk-table size, find the argmax shift.

A coupled-map learner whose global gain g is set by a slow modulator reading a running load estimate (prediction error): g is pushed toward the order-chaos boundary (lambda_max near 0) when load is high and toward contraction when load is low.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: the gain -> Lyapunov-exponent relation and the order-chaos boundary
concept_contributions.Cognitive Load Theory: the load signal that sets the target exponent
concept_contributions.Neuromodulation: the single slow scalar that moves g

knockouts.Chaos Theory: no exploration regime; gain only scales responsiveness
knockouts.Cognitive Load Theory: target g no longer depends on the task; reduces to fixed criticality
knockouts.Neuromodulation: g fixed; must be hand-tuned per task

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: a learning-rate or temperature schedule that anneals with error (simulated annealing)

questions.what_exists: N coupled maps, scalar g, load estimator
questions.what_is_selected: g values minimising error per task
questions.what_can_transfer: the g(load) policy to another map family
questions.distinguishing_observable: optimal lambda_max shifts monotonically with element interactivity at fixed error magnitude; annealing predicts dependence on error magnitude only

hypotheses.statement: Capacity = number of coexisting attractors in a globally coupled map; storing chunk k+1 fragments existing basins, and beyond a gain-dependent K* basins become riddled so cued recall fails.

concept_contributions.Cognitive Load Theory: the hard count limit and chunk-as-single-element
concept_contributions.Neuromodulation: gain moves the system between few large basins and many tiny ones

knockouts.Cognitive Load Theory: no reason to measure a count limit; becomes generic multistability
knockouts.Neuromodulation: K* fixed; no trade between capacity and search

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: Hopfield-style capacity limit from pattern interference, no chaos needed

questions.what_exists: globally coupled logistic maps, stored cluster patterns
questions.distinguishing_observable: basin-boundary dimension rises before recall fails; interference predicts smooth decline without a boundary-dimension precursor

hypotheses.statement: Chaotic itinerancy proposes candidate chunks (transient visits to attractor ruins); a phasic broadcast pulse on success locally lowers gain at currently active units, freezing the current ruin into a stable attractor. The capacity limit bounds how many ruins can be frozen before itinerancy stops.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: itinerancy as a free proposal generator

knockouts.Chaos Theory: proposals must come from external noise
knockouts.Cognitive Load Theory: unlimited freezing; itinerancy dies immediately or never
knockouts.Neuromodulation: no consolidation; itinerancy never becomes memory

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: random search with a success-triggered cache (epsilon-greedy with memory)

questions.what_exists: units in chaotic itinerancy, a pulse signal
questions.what_can_transfer: the library to tasks sharing sub-patterns
questions.distinguishing_observable: time-to-discovery follows ruin dwell-time statistics rather than the proposal count of an equivalent random search

hypotheses.statement: The modulator is swept slowly while tasks of increasing intrinsic load are presented; hysteresis near bifurcations makes easy-to-hard order retain more pattern structure than hard-to-easy, with identical total exposure.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: hysteresis and path dependence around bifurcations
concept_contributions.Cognitive Load Theory: ordering of tasks by intrinsic load
concept_contributions.Neuromodulation: the slow parameter whose path matters

knockouts.Cognitive Load Theory: tasks have no load ordering; becomes a generic parameter sweep
knockouts.Neuromodulation: parameter never moves; any order effect comes only from forcing

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: curriculum effect from interference/recency (last task wins)

questions.what_exists: coupled maps, forcing patterns, a modulator path
questions.what_persists: attractor set after forcing is removed
questions.what_is_selected: patterns imprinted under a matching modulator value
questions.distinguishing_observable: order effect vanishes in a monostable twin with matched variance, whereas recency predicts it persists there

hypotheses.statement: A scalar broadcast controller stabilises unstable periodic orbits with small parameter kicks computed from the last C observed states; the longest stabilisable period grows with C, so controller working memory bounds the repertoire a single modulator can pin.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: the UPO skeleton as a free repertoire of behaviours

knockouts.Chaos Theory: no UPOs; nothing cheap to stabilise
knockouts.Cognitive Load Theory: C unlimited; repertoire bounded only by noise
knockouts.Neuromodulation: kicks could be vector and site-specific; the question changes

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: a generic linear controller needs observation depth >= system order (observability); nothing chaos-specific

questions.what_exists: a chaotic map, a delay buffer of size C, a kick budget
questions.what_can_transfer: the p_max(C) law to other maps
questions.distinguishing_observable: sharp p_max threshold in C plus failure when fitted on time-shuffled data

hypotheses.statement: Extraneous load = input directions that project onto expanding Lyapunov directions and get amplified; modulation reshapes the Lyapunov spectrum direction-selectively (contracting irrelevant directions), acting as attention without addressing individual units.

concept_contributions.Neuromodulation: a global signal that nonetheless shapes the spectrum

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: input filtering by a learned gating mask

questions.what_exists: driven coupled maps with relevant and distractor inputs
questions.distinguishing_observable: angle between leading Lyapunov vectors and the distractor subspace grows under modulation, while a mask baseline leaves the spectrum unchanged

hypotheses.statement: Chunks are frequent words in the symbolic dynamics of a chaotic source; a learner with chunk budget C captures grammar only up to an entropy h*(C); moving source entropy (or sampling resolution) to h*(C) maximises learned structure.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: topological entropy and a grammar with forbidden words

knockouts.Chaos Theory: source i.i.d. or Markov; no grammar
knockouts.Cognitive Load Theory: unbounded table; argmax at maximal entropy

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: any n-gram learner does best on low-entropy sequences; an argmax shift could be a finite-sample effect

questions.what_exists: symbol sequence, chunk table of size C
questions.what_can_transfer: the h*(C) law to other maps
questions.distinguishing_observable: argmax entropy increases with C and learned gain exceeds a Markov-1 surrogate

hypotheses.statement: Two modulators (gain and temporal integration) interact; their cross-coupling, not the circuit, generates chaos, and load determines which modulator saturates first.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: chaos arising in the modulator loop itself

knockouts.Chaos Theory: modulators simply settle; weak dependency: chaos is incidental here

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: two coupled PID loops with windup oscillate; any two-integrator loop can oscillate

questions.distinguishing_observable: positive lambda in the modulator time series only when load exceeds capacity

hypotheses.statement: Elements bound into one chunk are chaotically synchronised clusters; capacity is the number of distinct synchronised clusters that can coexist; the modulator sets coupling and hence cluster count.

knockouts.Chaos Theory: periodic oscillators might give the same count; dependency possibly weak

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: phase coding of items in nested periodic rhythms gives a count limit without chaos

questions.distinguishing_observable: cluster-count limit differs between chaotic and matched periodic oscillators; if identical, chaos is decoration

hypotheses.statement: Load-induced chaos: held items compete (generalised Lotka-Volterra); beyond a threshold item count the competition becomes chaotic and items drop out; a modulator scaling inter-item interaction shifts the threshold.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: onset of chaos with dimension in competitive systems

knockouts.Chaos Theory: collapse must come from exclusion alone

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: competitive exclusion in non-chaotic (symmetric) competition removes items with no chaos

questions.what_can_transfer: the threshold law across random interaction matrices
questions.distinguishing_observable: within fixed n, chaotic draws lose more items than non-chaotic draws; the symmetric twin cannot be chaotic

hypotheses.statement: A population of chunk-programs evolves with a mutation rate set by a modulator tracking recent success; capacity caps population size; ruggedness from a chaotic fitness map sets the needed rate.

knockouts.Chaos Theory: weak dependency: chaos only supplies ruggedness
knockouts.Cognitive Load Theory: weak dependency: the cap is population size, not load

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: standard self-adaptive mutation rate (1/5 success rule)

questions.distinguishing_observable: almost none beyond the 1/5 rule; three-way dependency is weak, stated as such

hypotheses.statement: Finite-time Lyapunov exponents between input elements measure element interactivity for free: elements whose perturbations co-diverge interact; the modulator allocates capacity to high-FTLE groups, forming chunks of interacting elements.

concept_contributions.Cognitive Load Theory: element interactivity as the quantity to measure

knockouts.Chaos Theory: no divergence; interactivity must be learned otherwise

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: correlation or mutual-information clustering of inputs

questions.distinguishing_observable: FTLE grouping recovers interaction structure where pairwise correlation is zero (XOR-coupled elements)

hypotheses.statement: A chaotic memory trace drifts at rate lambda_max; periodic broadcast resets resynchronise it to a small stored anchor set; retention time ~ Lyapunov time x number of anchors under a fixed anchor budget.
hypotheses.simpler_alternative: periodic refresh of a leaky memory (rehearsal)

questions.distinguishing_observable: optimal reset interval scales with 1/lambda_max, whereas leak-based rehearsal scales with the leak constant

hypotheses.statement: In a population of fixed-gain agents facing time-varying load, adaptive modulation is selected only when load changes faster than the Lyapunov time of the agents' own dynamics.

concept_contributions.Chaos Theory: Lyapunov time as the agents' internal timescale

knockouts.Chaos Theory: no internal timescale; the threshold comes from other time constants

hypotheses.simpler_alternative: general result: plasticity is favoured when the environment varies on intermediate timescales

questions.distinguishing_observable: the selection threshold tracks Lyapunov time when it is varied independently of other time constants

The positive control failed: a single k=2 pattern forced 500 steps at a=3.7 left a final partition of ~3.7 clusters with mean ARI 0.024 against the pattern (threshold 0.8), so by the PREREG no reading of the treatment is made. lenses.name: Lyapunov budget ledger
lenses.rationale: Treat working capacity as a budget of expanding directions and tie chunk counts to the Kaplan-Yorke dimension.
lenses.sourceRepresentation: trajectory plus tangent dynamics of the learner
lenses.transformation: QR-based Lyapunov spectrum over windows; count positive exponents and KY dimension
predictedSignals: KY dimension tracks the number of held chunks
modulation reduces the positive count under load
lenses.nullExpectation: KY dimension unrelated to chunk count (rank correlation near 0)
lenses.informationAddedBeyondExistingLenses: ties a capacity count to a dynamical invariant rather than a task score

lenses.name: Basin census
lenses.rationale: Capacity claims are claims about basin counts and basin geometry.
lenses.transformation: sample initial conditions, cluster final states, estimate basin entropy and the uncertainty exponent of basin boundaries
predictedSignals: boundary dimension rises before recall fails
lenses.nullExpectation: attractor count flat in the modulator
lenses.informationAddedBeyondExistingLenses: gives a precursor that separates basin fragmentation from interference

lenses.name: Modulator hysteresis loop
lenses.rationale: Order effects attributed to hysteresis must come with a hysteresis loop in the modulator parameter.
lenses.sourceRepresentation: state versus a slowly swept modulator
lenses.transformation: sweep up then down; label attractor sets; compute loop area and up/down overlap
observables: overlap between up- and down-sweep attractor sets
predictedSignals: nonzero loop area where order effects appear
lenses.nullExpectation: zero loop area within seed noise

lenses.name: Chunk-budget grammar lens
lenses.rationale: Treat learning as compressing symbolic dynamics under a hard context-table cap.
lenses.sourceRepresentation: symbol sequence from a partition of the map
lenses.transformation: fit a capped context table; compare with a Markov-1 surrogate
predictedSignals: argmax entropy shifts with the cap
lenses.nullExpectation: gain curve independent of the cap
lenses.informationAddedBeyondExistingLenses: separates capacity matching from a generic low-entropy advantage

lenses.name: Overload onset spectroscopy
lenses.rationale: Add items one at a time and measure the dynamical regime alongside recall.
lenses.transformation: for each n compute lambda_max and survivor fraction over random interaction draws
observables: chaotic-vs-non-chaotic recall gap at fixed n
lenses.nullExpectation: recall independent of chaos at fixed n
lenses.informationAddedBeyondExistingLenses: tests whether overload is dynamical rather than combinatorial

lenses.name: Single-knob controllability
lenses.rationale: What can one scalar broadcast pin, given a finite memory of past states?
lenses.sourceRepresentation: chaotic map plus a scalar kick
lenses.transformation: fit feedback from C delayed states; attempt stabilisation of each UPO period
predictedSignals: p_max grows with C; shuffled-fit twin fails
lenses.informationAddedBeyondExistingLenses: gives a controller-memory account of a modulator's repertoire

experiments.hypothesis: Item loss under overload is caused by chaotic competition, not only by competitive exclusion.
experiments.mechanism: generalised Lotka-Volterra dx_i/dt = x_i(1 - sum_j A'_ij x_j) with A'_ii = 1 and A'_ij = m*A_ij, A_ij ~ U(0,1.5) asymmetric; modulator m scales off-diagonals
experiments.control: at the same n and m, compare chaotic draws (lambda_max > 1e-3) with non-chaotic draws
experiments.positive_control: screen random 4-species matrices for one with lambda_max > 0.01 and confirm the estimator reports a positive exponent from 5 initial conditions
experiments.observable: lambda_max by tangent-space QR over the last 2000 time units; recall = fraction of species with x_i > 1e-3 at the end
experiments.success_criterion: for n in 4..8 pooled, mean recall of chaotic draws is lower than non-chaotic draws by >= 0.15 with Mann-Whitney p < 0.01 after regressing out mean off-diagonal strength, AND lowering m from 1.0 to 0.6 raises n_recall* (smallest n with mean recall < 0.5) by >= 1 while reducing the chaotic fraction by >= 0.2
experiments.failure_criterion: recall gap < 0.05 or p > 0.05 (overload is exclusion, not chaos); or fewer than 20 chaotic draws in total (world cannot test the claim)
experiments.alternative_explanation: chaotic draws simply have stronger mean interaction, which causes both chaos and exclusion
experiments.null_twin: symmetrised matrices (A + A^T)/2 with matched off-diagonal mean and variance: they admit a Lyapunov function, cannot be chaotic, and still show exclusion
experiments.why_this_implementation: competition among held items is the literal CLT picture of interacting elements; ODE ecology keeps it non-ML
experiments.size: n = 2..10, 100 matrices per n, 5 m values, 3 initial-condition seeds, T = 5000 time units, dt = 0.01 RK4, vectorised numpy
stupid_explanations: chaotic draws have larger interaction strength (regress recall on mean A and chaos jointly)
the 1e-3 extinction threshold counts low-amplitude chaotic excursions as losses
integration error at dt = 0.01 manufactures positive exponents (repeat at dt = 0.005 on a subset)

experiments.hypothesis: The longest unstable periodic orbit a scalar-kick controller can stabilise is bounded by the number C of past states it holds.
experiments.mechanism: logistic map x' = (3.9 + u_t) x (1 - x) with |u_t| <= delta; controller u_t = sum_{k<C} w_k (x_{t-k} - x*_{phase,k}) fitted by least squares on 20000 uncontrolled points
experiments.intervention: C in 1..8, target period p in 1..8, delta = 0.02
experiments.control: controller fitted on a time-shuffled copy of the training series
experiments.positive_control: C = 16 stabilises periods 1..4 with success fraction >= 0.8
experiments.observable: success = |x_t - orbit| < 1e-3 for 200 consecutive steps within 5000 steps; success fraction over 50 trials
experiments.success_criterion: p_max(C) (largest p with success fraction >= 0.8) is nondecreasing in C and p_max(8) - p_max(1) >= 3; shuffled-fit twin success fraction <= 0.1 for all p >= 2
experiments.failure_criterion: p_max(8) - p_max(1) <= 1 (memory is not the binding resource), or shuffled twin succeeds >= 0.5 at some p >= 2 (control does not use the dynamics)
experiments.alternative_explanation: failures at long periods come from orbit-finding error or the kick budget, not memory
experiments.null_twin: time-shuffled training series: identical marginal distribution of x, temporal structure destroyed
experiments.why_this_implementation: a one-dimensional map makes UPOs enumerable; the controller is linear least squares, no learning system
experiments.size: 8 C values x 8 periods x 50 trials x 5000 steps
stupid_explanations: delta too small for longer orbits regardless of C (repeat at delta = 0.05)
long-period UPOs located inaccurately
trajectory lands near the orbit by luck (compare waiting time to uncontrolled recurrence)

statistics.treatment: not built (pilot failed twice; no treatment statistic exists)

anomalies.text: Null twin never shows the memory law (p_max=0 at every C in both attempts) but a shuffled-fit controller stabilises whole cells (50/50 trials) in single seeds: a random proportional gain lands in the finite stabilising interval of a 1-D UPO. Pooled null fraction exceeded the spec's 0.1 twin bound at p>=2 in both attempts (0.2, then 0.4 after the intercept repair).
Spec's control and null_twin are the same construction (time-shuffled fit); both would be affected.

Positive control at C=16 already reached 1.0 at p=1..4; with a 1-D map a C=1 deadbeat controller is sufficient in principle (M5's own simpler_alternative: observability needs depth >= system order = 1). Not measured: no treatment run.

experiments.hypothesis: With identical exposure, presenting low-load patterns first under a rising modulator retains more pattern structure than the reverse order, because of hysteresis.
experiments.mechanism: globally coupled logistic maps x_i' = (1 - eps) f_a(x_i) + eps * mean_j f_a(x_j) + b_i, N = 100, eps = 0.1; forcing patterns b with k in {2, 4, 8} distinct levels (amplitude 0.02); modulator a ramps with k
experiments.intervention: easy->hard (k = 2, 4, 8 at a = 3.7, 3.8, 3.9) versus hard->easy (k = 8, 4, 2 at a = 3.9, 3.8, 3.7), 500 steps each, then 1000 unforced steps
experiments.control: same patterns and orders with a fixed at 3.8
experiments.positive_control: single pattern k = 2 at a = 3.7 is retained (adjusted Rand index >= 0.8)
experiments.observable: retention = mean over the three patterns of the adjusted Rand index between the final cluster partition and each pattern's partition
experiments.success_criterion: mean retention(easy->hard) - retention(hard->easy) >= 0.15 over 30 seeds with Wilcoxon p < 0.01, AND the same difference in the null twin < 0.05, AND L3 loop area > 0 across a in [3.7, 3.9]
experiments.failure_criterion: difference < 0.05, or null-twin difference >= 0.1 (order effect is recency or interference, not hysteresis)
experiments.alternative_explanation: the last pattern dominates (recency) and happens to be easier to retain in one order
experiments.null_twin: replace f_a with a contracting affine map whose per-site variance matches the chaotic run: monostable, no hysteresis
experiments.why_this_implementation: coupled maps give multistable cluster states without any neural learning rule
experiments.size: N = 100, 30 seeds, 2 orders + fixed-a control + null twin, 2500 steps per run
stupid_explanations: recency of the final pattern
adjusted Rand index biased by cluster count
transients not settled after 1000 steps (check with 5000)

anomalies.text: positive control not retained: mean ARI 0.024 < 0.8 (mean clusters 3.7)
TREATMENT orders end in different regimes: easy->hard (unforced at a=3.9) mean 90.6 clusters, hard->easy (unforced at a=3.7) mean 3.8 clusters; fixed-a CONTROL at 3.8 ~100 clusters (turbulent)

instrument repair declined: no readout defect found; the positive control fails because the specified dynamics at a=3.7 collapse to ~4 clusters unrelated to the pattern, and any change to amplitude/eps/steps would be tuning the mechanism

experiments.hypothesis: A learner with chunk budget C extracts most structure from a chaotic source whose entropy is matched to C, and the matched entropy rises with C.
experiments.mechanism: logistic map at 20 r values in [3.57, 4.0], binary partition at 0.5; learner = variable-order context table capped at C contexts (most frequent kept)
experiments.control: the same learner trained on a Markov-1 surrogate with matched symbol and transition frequencies
experiments.positive_control: C = 1024 achieves gain >= 0.1 over the surrogate at some r
experiments.observable: gain = next-symbol accuracy on 20000 held-out symbols of the capped table minus that of the surrogate-trained table; entropy from block-entropy slope
experiments.success_criterion: median over 10 seeds of the entropy at argmax gain strictly increases across C = 4, 16, 64, AND gain at argmax >= 0.05 for C >= 16
experiments.failure_criterion: argmax entropy identical for all C, or gain at argmax < 0.02 (first-order statistics explain everything)
experiments.alternative_explanation: periodic windows in r create predictability spikes unrelated to capacity matching
experiments.null_twin: Markov-1 surrogate sequences: matched symbol and pair frequencies, higher-order grammar destroyed
experiments.why_this_implementation: the context-table cap is a direct CLT capacity bound; no neural predictor
experiments.size: 20 r values x 3 C values x 10 seeds x 100000 symbols
stupid_explanations: periodic windows in r
finite training length favours low-entropy sources
the eviction rule, not cap size, sets the argmax

experiments.hypothesis: At a fixed number of held items (n = 4) and matched interaction strength, competitive dynamics that are chaotic lose more items than competitive dynamics that are not chaotic: item loss under load is caused by chaotic competition, not only by competitive exclusion.
experiments.mechanism: Competitive generalised Lotka-Volterra dx_i/dt = r_i x_i (1 - sum_j A_ij x_j), n = 4, r = (1, 0.72, 1.53, 1.27). A is drawn from a neighbourhood of the Vano et al. (2006) chaotic matrix A0 = [[1,1.09,1.52,0],[0,1,0.44,1.36],[2.33,0,1,0.47],[1.21,0.51,0.35,1]]: every nonzero off-diagonal entry is multiplied by an independent U(0.9, 1.1) factor; zeros and the unit diagonal are kept. The neighbourhood contains both chaotic and non-chaotic draws at nearly identical interaction strength. Initial state x0 ~ U(0.2, 0.4)^4 per draw.
experiments.intervention: None is imposed on the dynamics; the contrast is the naturally occurring chaos label of each draw: chaotic if lambda_max > 0.005, measured by a renormalised twin trajectory (delta0 = 1e-8, renormalised every 1.0 time unit) over t in [300, 1500], RK4 dt = 0.05. The same draw is then integrated, unmodified, to t = 3000.
experiments.control: Symmetrised draws (A + A^T)/2, integrated identically: these admit a Lyapunov function, cannot be chaotic, and give the loss rate from exclusion alone; reported descriptively, no clause.
experiments.positive_control: Effect present by construction: same family and same phase-A integration and chaos label, but on t in [1500, 3000] an absorbing boundary removes permanently any species whose abundance falls below 0.02, so the large excursions of chaotic draws cost items by construction. Recall and clauses computed exactly as for the treatment.
experiments.observable: Per draw: chaos label (above) and recall = fraction of the 4 species whose mean abundance over t in [2800, 3000] exceeds 1e-3; mean off-diagonal strength = mean of the 12 off-diagonal entries of A. Pooled over 5 seeds x 100 draws.
experiments.success_criterion: [{"id": "S1", "text": "Pooled mean recall of non-chaotic draws minus pooled mean recall of chaotic draws is at least 0.08 (0.32 species of 4).", "statistic": "mean(recall | non-chaotic) - mean(recall | chaotic), pooled 500 draws", "comparison": ">=", "threshold": 0.08}, {"id": "S2", "text": "One-sided Mann-Whitney U test (non-chaotic recall greater than chaotic recall) has p below 0.01.", "statistic": "Mann-Whitney U one-sided p-value, pooled", "comparison": "<", "threshold": 0.01}, {"id": "S3", "text": "In the OLS regression recall ~ 1 + mean_offdiag_strength + chaotic, the negated coefficient of the chaotic indicator is at least 0.06 (the chaos effect survives adjustment for interaction strength).", "statistic": "-beta_chaotic from OLS recall ~ 1 + strength + chaotic, pooled", "comparison": ">=", "threshold": 0.06}]
experiments.failure_criterion: [{"id": "F1", "text": "The recall gap is below 0.03 (about 1.4 standard errors of the label-permutation null): overload loss is exclusion, not chaos.", "statistic": "mean(recall | non-chaotic) - mean(recall | chaotic), pooled", "comparison": "<", "threshold": 0.03}, {"id": "F2", "text": "Adjusted chaos coefficient below 0.02: any raw gap is carried by interaction strength.", "statistic": "-beta_chaotic from OLS recall ~ 1 + strength + chaotic, pooled", "comparison": "<", "threshold": 0.02}, {"id": "F3", "text": "Fewer than 20 chaotic or fewer than 20 non-chaotic draws: the world cannot test the claim (UNTESTABLE, not NULL).", "statistic": "min(n_chaotic, n_nonchaotic), pooled", "comparison": "<", "threshold": 20}]
experiments.alternative_explanation: Chaotic draws differ systematically from non-chaotic neighbours in interaction strength or in which entries were perturbed, and that difference, not chaos, causes (or prevents) exclusion; or the 1e-3 floor counts low chaotic excursions as losses.
experiments.null_twin: Label-permutation twin: the treatment's own rows with the chaos labels permuted within each seed (fixed permutation seed 1000 + seed). Every nuisance statistic is identical (same draws, same recall values, same number of chaotic labels); only the association between chaos and recall is destroyed. A second, physical twin (symmetrised matrices) is the control arm.
experiments.cost_estimate: about 0.2 CPU core-minutes for the treatment (controls took 0.12 core-minutes)
stupid_explanations: chaotic draws have different mean interaction strength (S3 adjusts for it; also report strength by class)
the 1e-3 floor on a 200-unit mean abundance misreads a slow chaotic excursion as a loss (report per-class minimum of mean abundance of surviving species)
lambda_max > 0.005 mislabels long transients or slow limit cycles as chaos (report lambda histogram; the unperturbed Vano matrix gives 0.019 and its symmetrisation -0.13 in the estimator check)
integration error at dt = 0.05 manufactures or hides chaos (repeat 50 draws at dt = 0.025 and compare labels)

experiments.hypothesis: Finite-time co-divergence of perturbations in a chaotic carrier recovers which elements interact (element interactivity) even when the interaction is XOR-like, so that pairwise correlation carries no grouping information, and it does so in the presence of a weak unstructured global leak.
experiments.mechanism: N = 12 units v_i in [-1, 1], nominal partition into 4 groups of 3. v_i' = (1 - kappa - eps_g) T(v_i) + kappa * v_p(i) * v_q(i) + eps_g * mean_j T(v_j), with T(v) = 4 v^3 - 3 v (odd cubic Chebyshev map, chaotic, symmetric invariant density), kappa = 0.10, eps_g = 0.05. In the treatment p(i), q(i) are the other two members of unit i's group: interaction is a product (XOR-like) of the partners, so partners are uncorrelated to first order; the global mean-field leak eps_g couples every unit to every other unit without group structure.
experiments.intervention: Readout applied to the treatment world: FTLE grouping. At K = 100 base times (burn-in 500 steps, spacing 20) each unit i is perturbed by delta = 1e-9 and both copies are iterated tau = 8 steps; D_ij = mean over base times of log10(|dv_j| + 1e-18); similarity D + D^T (diagonal set to the maximum); average-linkage agglomeration into 4 clusters; adjusted Rand index (ARI) against the nominal partition.
experiments.control: Correlation grouping on the same trajectory: similarity = max(|Pearson lag 0|, |Pearson lag 1| in either direction) over 5000 post-burn-in steps; same clustering; ARI against the nominal partition. This is M12's simpler alternative.
experiments.positive_control: Effect present by construction: identical world and readouts with eps_g = 0, so perturbations can travel only inside groups and FTLE grouping must recover the partition; the product coupling keeps correlation near zero.
experiments.observable: Per seed: ari_ftle, ari_corr (both against the nominal 4 x 3 partition). Statistics are means over 10 seeds (initial condition v0 ~ U(-1, 1)^12 from numpy default_rng(seed)).
experiments.success_criterion: [{"id": "S1", "text": "Mean over 10 seeds of the FTLE-grouping ARI is at least 0.8.", "statistic": "mean_seed(ari_ftle)", "comparison": ">=", "threshold": 0.8}, {"id": "S2", "text": "Mean over 10 seeds of (FTLE-grouping ARI minus correlation-grouping ARI) is at least 0.5.", "statistic": "mean_seed(ari_ftle - ari_corr)", "comparison": ">=", "threshold": 0.5}]
experiments.failure_criterion: [{"id": "F1", "text": "Mean FTLE-grouping ARI below 0.3: co-divergence does not isolate interacting elements once an unstructured leak is present.", "statistic": "mean_seed(ari_ftle)", "comparison": "<", "threshold": 0.3}, {"id": "F2", "text": "Mean (FTLE ARI minus correlation ARI) below 0.2: the correlation baseline does as well, so FTLE adds nothing here.", "statistic": "mean_seed(ari_ftle - ari_corr)", "comparison": "<", "threshold": 0.2}]
experiments.alternative_explanation: Any perturbation-response (causal intervention) readout recovers a coupling graph whether or not the carrier is chaotic; success would show that intervention beats observation, not that chaos is what measures interactivity. Separately, the global leak may synchronise units so that every readout sees one block.
experiments.null_twin: Same map, same kappa = 0.10, same eps_g = 0.05, same in-degree 2 product coupling, but each unit's two partners drawn uniformly at random from the other 11 units (default_rng(500 + seed)); the nominal partition remains the scoring target. Nuisance statistics (coupling count, strength, map, leak) matched; group structure destroyed.
experiments.cost_estimate: about 0.02 CPU core-minutes for the treatment (all controls took 0.03)
stupid_explanations: the leak synchronises units (check corr_between_mean and trajectory range; the twin at eps_g = 0.05 stays unsynchronised, mean |corr| about 0.04)
the ARI of a 4-cluster average-linkage partition is inflated by cluster-size artefacts (report the partitions; chance ARI in the twins is about 0)
the invariant density is not symmetric, so E[v] != 0 and product coupling leaks first-order correlation (report corr_within_mean vs corr_between_mean)
tau = 8 is either too short for within-group spread or long enough for the leak to saturate everything (report ftle_within_mean and ftle_between_mean)
